interactions.summary: A student answers Jiang's setup question by saying Dante was probably not a healthy person.
Jiang speculates that Dante was sickly, visionary, and kept alive by the will to finish the Divine Comedy, while also entertaining the opposite causal story that the labor of the poem exhausted him.

A student challenges Dante's use of prophecy as wishy-washy self-framing, asking how his attitude toward predetermination should be understood when the events had already happened by the time of writing.

Jiang answers that Dante is not consoling himself retroactively but giving readers hope by making exile feel preordained and therefore not their fault, which allows peace, self-forgiveness, and forgiveness of others.
A student says the next psychological step is accepting fate.
A second voice briefly affirms the student's point without adding content.

claims.claim: Jiang speculates that Dante may have been chronically ill, bedridden, and visionary, and that this bodily condition partly explains both the poem's visions and the timing of his death.
Jiang says the Divine Comedy may have prolonged Dante's life because his will to finish the poem kept him going.
Jiang says Dante writes prophetic exile scenes to give readers hope rather than merely to console himself.
Jiang says the deepest comfort of preordination is learning that exile is not your fault, which removes the core source of trauma.
Jiang compares Dante's release from blame to children traumatized by divorce, arguing that the wound depends on believing the catastrophe was your fault.
Jiang says once Dante knows God knows the exile was not his fault, he can rest, forgive himself, and forgive others.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang provocatively flips causality and suggests the Divine Comedy may not have killed Dante but actually kept him alive.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if it weren't for Divine Comedy, he'd probably be dead at 40
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns poetic vocation into a life-sustaining force instead of a merely expressive activity.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang says the poem's prophecy exists for us because readers are meant to become Dante and inherit hope instead of despair.
signature_moments.source_phrase: we are Dante in the poem
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It states the strongest reader-identification claim in the packet and explains why Dante's self-prophecy matters.

signature_moments.moment: The lecture's psychology hardens around a single thesis: trauma comes from blaming yourself for what was not your fault.
signature_moments.source_phrase: If they think it's their fault
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It links exile, prophecy, childhood trauma, and consolation into one explanatory mechanism.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's term for the exile being written into a providential order, which strips it of personal guilt.
Used psychologically: catastrophe wounds most deeply when the sufferer internalizes blame.
The inward consequence Jiang draws from learning that God does not assign Dante guilt for exile.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-17 Jiang makes Dante's predictive framing serve a pastoral-psychological function: prophecy is valuable because it transforms exile from traumatic self-accusation into forgiven participation in providence.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang presents Dante's sickness, dream-life, and lifespan counterfactuals as speculative possibilities rather than firmly sourced biographical facts.
The one-word affirmation is preserved only as a minimal interaction because it carries no stable conceptual content.
